title: Knowledge Graph
shortDefinition: A structured representation of entities and their relationships as a connected network for AI reasoning.
definition: A knowledge graph is a structured representation of entities (people, products, organizations, concepts) and the relationships between them, organized as a connected network rather than a flat table or document collection. Knowledge graphs let AI systems reason about explicit relationships — 'this product was manufactured by this company, which was acquired by this parent company' — in ways that pure text search or vector similarity alone don't capture well.

sections.title: How knowledge graphs work
sections.description: Knowledge graphs store information as nodes (entities) connected by edges (relationships).

content.text: A knowledge graph stores information as nodes (entities) connected by edges (relationships) — for example, a 'Company' node connected to a 'Product' node via a 'manufactures' relationship, which in turn connects to a 'Customer' node via a 'purchased' relationship. This structure allows queries that traverse multiple relationship hops ('find all customers affected by a recall of products manufactured by subsidiaries of this parent company') that would be difficult to answer from unstructured documents or simple keyword search alone.

content.title: Key components of a knowledge graph:
items: Nodes — entities (people, products, organizations, concepts).
Edges — relationships connecting entities ('manufactures,' 'located in,' 'acquired').
Properties — attributes of nodes and edges ('founded in 1998,' 'has 500 employees').
Query traversal — ability to follow multiple relationship hops.
Reasoning — inference based on graph structure and relationships.

content.title: The key insight
content.text: Knowledge graphs don't just store facts — they store connections. This lets AI reason about relationships, not just retrieve similar content.

sections.title: Knowledge graphs vs. vector databases: different strengths

content.text: Vector databases excel at finding semantically similar content — 'find documents about a similar topic.' Knowledge graphs excel at representing and reasoning about explicit, structured relationships between specific entities — 'find everything connected to this specific entity through these specific relationship types.' Many sophisticated RAG and enterprise search systems combine both: using a knowledge graph to understand entity relationships and structure complex queries, and a vector database for semantic similarity search across unstructured content, sometimes called 'graph RAG.'

content.title: Graph RAG
content.text: Graph RAG combines knowledge graphs with vector search: the knowledge graph structures relationship queries, while vector search retrieves relevant unstructured content for grounding.

sections.title: Limitations and risks of knowledge graphs

content.text: Knowledge graphs are powerful but have limitations. Building and maintaining them is complex and resource-intensive, especially from unstructured data. They require ongoing updates as the source data changes, and extraction pipelines can introduce errors that propagate through the graph. Graph query performance can degrade with scale, and not all use cases benefit from the added complexity of relationship reasoning.

items: Construction complexity: building graphs from unstructured data is challenging.
Maintenance overhead: graphs need ongoing updates as data changes.
Extraction errors: entity and relationship extraction can introduce errors.
Query performance: graph queries can be slow at large scale.
Not always needed: many use cases don't require graph reasoning.
Data quality dependency: graph quality depends on source data quality.
Skill requirements: graph construction requires specialized expertise.

content.title: Important
content.text: Knowledge graphs are powerful tools, but they're not for every use case. They're best for applications that genuinely require multi-hop relationship reasoning.

sections.title: Best practices for knowledge graph implementation

content.text: Building an effective knowledge graph requires careful entity identification, relationship modeling, and validation. The following practices can help ensure your knowledge graph delivers valuable reasoning capabilities.

content.title: Recommended approach:
items: Start with a clear understanding of the relationship queries you need to support.
Identify key entity types and relationship types for your domain.
Build extraction pipelines for entities and relationships from your data.
Validate extraction accuracy against a representative sample.
Design graph schema with flexibility for future additions.
Implement ongoing sync pipelines to keep the graph current.
Test query performance and optimize for your expected volume.
Consider combining with vector search for unstructured content.

content.title: Key metric
content.text: Measure query recall and precision on representative relationship queries. If the graph can't answer multi-hop questions accurately, it's not delivering value.

faqs.title: Frequently asked questions about knowledge graphs

items.question: What's a real-world example of when a knowledge graph adds value?
items.answer: Understanding supply chain relationships across multiple supplier tiers, tracing regulatory compliance obligations across related corporate entities, or answering questions that require multi-hop reasoning across connected records.

items.question: Can a knowledge graph be combined with RAG and an LLM?
items.answer: Yes, this combination (sometimes called graph RAG) lets the system use relationship traversal to find relevant entities, then generates natural language answers grounded in both the graph structure and retrieved text.

items.question: Does building a knowledge graph require manually mapping every relationship?
items.answer: Not entirely — ClickMasters uses automated extraction from existing structured and unstructured data, validated by your team, rather than requiring fully manual graph construction.

items.question: How does a knowledge graph stay current as our data changes?
items.answer: ClickMasters builds ongoing sync pipelines that update the graph as underlying source data changes, similar to how a vector database is kept current.

items.question: How long does a knowledge graph project take?
items.answer: 10–28 weeks depending on data complexity and whether ongoing sync infrastructure is included.

items.question: Is a knowledge graph overkill for a simple internal Q&A tool?
items.answer: Often yes — ClickMasters recommends the simplest approach (typically standard RAG) that meets your accuracy requirements, reserving knowledge graphs for use cases genuinely requiring relationship reasoning.

items.question: What is the difference between a knowledge graph and an ontology?
items.answer: An ontology defines the types of entities and relationships that exist in a domain (a schema). A knowledge graph is an instance of that ontology with actual data. Ontologies provide the structure; knowledge graphs provide the populated content.

items.question: What are popular technologies for building knowledge graphs?
items.answer: Common technologies include graph databases (Neo4j, Amazon Neptune, TigerGraph), RDF stores (Apache Jena, GraphDB), and knowledge graph frameworks (like RDFlib). ClickMasters selects the right technology based on your scale and query patterns.

items.question: How does a knowledge graph improve RAG performance?
items.answer: A knowledge graph improves RAG by enabling relationship-aware retrieval. Instead of retrieving based on similarity alone, the system can traverse relationships to find connected entities, which is especially valuable for questions that involve multiple related concepts or multi-step reasoning.

items.question: What are the challenges of extracting knowledge graphs from unstructured text?
items.answer: Challenges include entity ambiguity (identifying the correct entity among many), relationship extraction (determining relationship types and directions), coreference resolution (linking mentions of the same entity), and scaling the extraction to large document sets with acceptable accuracy.
